Name: early_answer_commitment_direction
Title: The Commit Vector: A Linear Direction Marking When a Reasoning Model Has Decided
Short Hypothesis: There exists a low-dimensional linear direction in the residual stream that activates when the model has internally committed to a final answer, often well before the CoT verbally concludes. Detecting this 'commit vector' lets us terminate reasoning early with calibrated confidence.
Related Work: Logit-lens/tuned-lens (nostalgebraist; Belrose et al. 2023) track answer emergence; Zhang et al. (2024) study early-exit for LLMs; Halawi et al. (2024) find overthinking directions. We differ by isolating a single causal, steerable 'commitment' direction validated by intervention (adding it accelerates commitment; ablating it delays it), not merely a decoding-time observation of answer stabilization.
Abstract: Reasoning models frequently 'know' the answer long before their chain-of-thought terminates, wasting compute on redundant verification. We hypothesize the existence of a linear commitment direction in the residual stream whose activation signals internal answer decision. We locate candidate directions via difference-in-means between activations at positions after which the answer never changes versus before, and via logistic probes trained to predict answer stability. We then causally validate: projecting activations onto the direction predicts the earliest safe exit point; adding the direction as a steering vector induces earlier commitment; ablating it prolongs deliberation. We build an early-exit controller that monitors the commit-vector projection and halts CoT when it crosses a calibrated threshold, trading a tunable accuracy budget for large token savings. We measure the token-savings/accuracy Pareto frontier against entropy-based and confidence-based baselines. We test universality across math, logic, and code, and across model sizes, asking whether the direction is shared. Success yields both an interpretability result (reasoning termination is linearly encoded) and a practical adaptive-compute method grounded in mechanism rather than heuristics.
Experiments: 1. Collect traces on GSM8K/MATH/BBH with per-token intermediate answer extraction (forced-answer probing at each position). 2. Label positions by answer stability (last position after which answer is fixed). 3. Fit difference-in-means and logistic probes per layer to find the commit direction; report probe AUC across layers. 4. Causal tests: add +alpha*direction, measure shift in stabilization position; ablate (project out), measure delay. 5. Build threshold-based early-exit; sweep threshold to trace accuracy vs mean tokens. 6. Compare against max-softmax-confidence and predictive-entropy early exit. 7. Cross-model/cross-task transfer of the fitted direction (cosine similarity, zero-shot exit performance).
Risk Factors and Limitations: Forced-answer probing may itself change behavior; 'commitment' may be multi-directional or nonlinear. Early exit could hurt hard problems disproportionately (safety of thresholding). The direction may reflect answer confidence rather than genuine commitment. Cross-model transfer may fail, limiting universality claims.
